title: Antiemetics in Surgery
subject: Surgery
summary: Antiemetics are drugs that stop nausea and vomiting, common after anaesthesia, opioids or abdominal surgery. Choosing the right agent depends on the cause, route, and safety in low‑resource settings.

sections.p: Vomiting is the forceful expulsion of stomach contents through the mouth. In surgery it is usually drug‑induced, anaesthetic‑related, or due to ileus or obstruction.
b: Identify cause: opioid use, anaesthetic agents, bowel obstruction, metabolic derangement, infection

sections.p: Use the Post‑operative Nausea and Vomiting (PONV) risk score: 0–2 low, 3–4 moderate, ≥5 high. Severe vomiting leads to dehydration, electrolyte loss and wound dehiscence.
In low‑resource East African hospitals the top causes are:

Patients report a sour taste, retching, and a sudden urge to vomit. Physical exam may show abdominal distension, tenderness, or signs of obstruction. Vital signs may reveal tachycardia or hypotension if dehydration is severe.
Investigations are guided by the suspected cause and available resources.

t.b: Rule out malaria as a systemic cause of nausea

sections.p: Urgent causes of vomiting that need immediate attention include obstruction, perforation, severe electrolyte imbalance, and haemorrhage.
b: Signs of peritonitis, severe abdominal pain, inability to keep fluids, or blood in vomitus

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then give antiemetics and supportive care.
b: If opioid‑induced: switch to non‑opioid analgesia (NSAIDs, paracetamol)
If anaesthetic: optimise ventilation, consider anti‑emetic prophylaxis
If obstruction/ileus: nil per os, NG suction, surgical consult
If metabolic: correct electrolytes, give glucose if hypoglycaemic

t.b: Reduces motion sickness and postoperative nausea, but avoid in glaucoma or prostatic hypertrophy

sections.p: Monitor hydration, electrolytes, and pain control. Preventive antiemetics are given to high‑risk patients (PONV score ≥3).
b: Use scopolamine patch 1.5 days pre‑op for motion‑sickness prone patients

sections.p: Post‑operative nausea can be mistaken for early sepsis, hypovolaemia, or opioid withdrawal.
b: Sepsis: fever, tachycardia, hypotension – differentiate by WCC, CRP, and source

sections.p: Normal electrolytes may be falsely reassuring if sampling is delayed after vomiting. A normal abdominal X‑ray does not exclude ileus.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal pain with vomiting, blood in vomitus, inability to keep fluids, signs of shock (hypotension, tachycardia), or persistent vomiting >24 h

faq.q: Why is ondansetron preferred over metoclopramide in the post‑operative period?
faq.a: Ondansetron blocks 5‑HT3 receptors with minimal CNS effects, making it safer for patients with delirium or seizures, and it does not cause extrapyramidal symptoms.

faq.q: Can scopolamine patch be used in a patient with glaucoma?
faq.a: No, scopolamine is contraindicated in narrow‑angle glaucoma because it can precipitate acute attacks.

faq.q: What is the first step if a patient vomits after receiving pethidine?
faq.a: Stop the opioid, give a non‑opioid analgesic (NSAID or paracetamol) and administer an antiemetic such as metoclopramide or ondansetron.

exam: A 65‑year‑old male develops vomiting 2 h after laparotomy for bowel obstruction. What is the most appropriate next step? — Stop opioids, start ondansetron, and NG suction to relieve obstruction.
A patient with postoperative nausea refuses antiemetics. What is a safe alternative? — Offer a scopolamine patch if no contraindications, or give a non‑opioid analgesic to reduce opioid use.
A 30‑year‑old woman vomits after receiving morphine for pain. She has a history of Parkinson’s disease. Which antiemetic is safest? — Ondansetron, as metoclopramide can worsen Parkinsonian symptoms.

You suspect ileus in a patient with vomiting and abdominal distension but the X‑ray is normal. What should you do? — Continue supportive care, monitor electrolytes, and consider surgical review if no improvement in 24 h.
A patient with malaria presents with vomiting and hypokalaemia. Which antiemetic is contraindicated? — Metoclopramide, because it can worsen hypokalaemia‑related cardiac arrhythmias.
A 50‑year‑old patient with postoperative vomiting has a QT interval of 480 ms. Which antiemetic should be avoided? — Ondansetron, due to risk of QT prolongation.
A patient with postoperative nausea is also on a beta‑blocker. Which antiemetic is least likely to interact? — Ondansetron, as it has minimal drug‑drug interactions.
A patient develops vomiting after receiving a 5‑HT3 antagonist. What is the likely mechanism? — Receptor up‑regulation or tachyphylaxis; consider switching to a dopamine antagonist.
